section_content.title: Corporate Objectives & Strategy

body.text: A **mission statement** communicates the core purpose and values of a business to stakeholders. It answers the question: why does this firm exist beyond making money? A strong mission aligns employees, attracts like-minded customers, and guides long-term decision-making.

Objectives translate the mission into concrete goals. **SMART objectives** are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. A hierarchy exists: the corporate objective sits at the top, departmental objectives sit below, and individual targets cascade down — ensuring every employee's work connects to the firm's overall direction.

The hierarchy of objectives creates alignment. The corporate objective might be 'increase market share to 25% within three years', which filters down into a marketing objective of launching two new campaigns per quarter and a production objective of reducing unit costs by 8%.

steps: Mission defines purpose
Corporate objectives set measurable goals
Departmental targets cascade down
Individual KPIs align to departments
body.result: Whole organisation pulls in the same direction

sections.title: Mission Statements & SMART Objectives
sections.keyIdea: A mission statement sets the direction; SMART objectives turn that direction into measurable targets — without both, strategy is either vague dreaming or aimless box-ticking.
sections.examMatters: Examiners often ask you to evaluate whether a mission statement has real strategic value or is just PR. Strong answers distinguish between firms where the mission genuinely shapes decisions (Patagonia's environmental focus) and firms where it is a vague slogan with no operational impact.

realExample.text: Tesla's mission is to 'accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy'. This drives every corporate objective — from scaling EV production to expanding the Supercharger network — and filters down to engineering targets for battery range and cost reduction.

sections.misconception: Students list SMART criteria without explaining why they matter. Wrong — the point is not the acronym itself but that vague goals cannot be measured or evaluated. Instead write: SMART objectives allow a firm to track progress, hold managers accountable, and adjust strategy when targets are missed.

body.text: **SWOT analysis** is a strategic planning tool that audits a firm's position. **Strengths** and **weaknesses** are internal factors the firm can control — brand reputation, workforce skills, financial reserves. **Opportunities** and **threats** are external factors it cannot control — market trends, competitor actions, regulatory changes.

The real value of SWOT is in the cross-analysis. A strength matched to an opportunity suggests an aggressive growth strategy. A weakness exposed to a threat signals a defensive priority. Without this matching, SWOT becomes a static list rather than a dynamic decision-making tool.

SWOT has limitations. It is subjective — two managers may categorise the same factor differently. It offers a snapshot, not a moving picture, so it dates quickly in fast-changing markets. It does not prioritise: listing twenty strengths and three threats gives no guidance on which matter most.

steps: Audit internal strengths & weaknesses
Scan external opportunities & threats
Match strengths to opportunities
Address weaknesses exposed to threats
body.result: Informed strategic choices — but only if the analysis is acted upon

sections.title: SWOT Analysis
sections.keyIdea: SWOT maps a firm's internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats — it is a starting point for strategy, not a strategy itself.
sections.examMatters: When asked to conduct a SWOT for a case study firm, examiners reward specificity. Do not write generic points like 'strong brand'. Instead write context-specific points drawn from the case data and link each factor to a strategic implication.

realExample.text: A SWOT of Netflix might identify strengths (global brand, data-driven content), weaknesses (high debt from original content spend), opportunities (growth in Asian markets), and threats (password-sharing crackdowns alienating users, Disney+ competition). The value is in matching: Netflix's data strength meets the Asian growth opportunity.

sections.misconception: Students present SWOT as a conclusion. Wrong — SWOT is an analytical starting point, not an answer. Instead write: SWOT identifies the strategic position; the firm must then choose a strategy (e.g. Ansoff's matrix or Porter's strategies) to act on what the SWOT reveals.

takeaway: Mission statements set purpose; SMART objectives make it measurable and actionable.
The hierarchy of objectives ensures corporate goals cascade into every department and role.
SWOT maps position but is a starting point — match strengths to opportunities to generate strategy.
SWOT is subjective and static; always acknowledge these limitations in evaluation.

section_content.title: Strategic Direction

body.text: **Ansoff's matrix** provides four growth strategies. **Market penetration** (existing product, existing market) is lowest risk — the firm grows by increasing market share through marketing, pricing, or loyalty schemes. **Product development** (new product, existing market) uses the firm's knowledge of its customers to introduce something new.

**Market development** (existing product, new market) takes a proven product to new geographies or demographics. **Diversification** (new product, new market) is highest risk because the firm has no existing knowledge of either the product or the customer base.

The strategic choice depends on context. A saturated market pushes a firm towards product development or market development. A firm with strong R&D capability may favour product development. Diversification is rare and often driven by a desire to spread risk across unrelated industries.

steps: Firm identifies growth opportunity
Plots option on Ansoff's matrix
Assesses risk vs reward
Matches to internal capabilities
body.result: Strategic direction chosen with awareness of risk level

sections.title: Ansoff's Matrix
sections.keyIdea: Ansoff's matrix organises growth options by two dimensions — existing vs new products and existing vs new markets — with risk increasing as the firm moves away from what it already knows.
sections.examMatters: Examiners expect you to apply Ansoff's matrix to a given firm, not just describe it. For a case study, identify which quadrant the firm's strategy falls into, explain why that level of risk is appropriate given the firm's position, and evaluate whether an alternative quadrant might be better.

realExample.text: Amazon's history maps perfectly onto Ansoff's matrix. It began with market penetration (more book buyers), moved to product development (Kindle, AWS), pursued market development (international expansion), and achieved diversification (Whole Foods grocery acquisition, healthcare entry).

sections.misconception: Students describe the four quadrants without linking risk to the firm's capabilities. Wrong — diversification is not always the worst choice; it depends on the firm's resources. Instead write: risk increases diagonally across the matrix, but a firm with strong capabilities and deep pockets may manage diversification better than a weaker firm handles market penetration in a declining market.

body.text: **Cost leadership** means being the lowest-cost producer in the industry. The firm achieves this through economies of scale, efficient operations, and tight cost control, then either undercuts rivals on price or matches their price for higher margins. This requires high volume and relentless operational efficiency.

**Differentiation** means offering something perceived as unique — design, brand, quality, innovation, or customer service — that justifies a premium price. The firm earns above-average returns because customers are willing to pay more. This requires sustained investment in R&D, marketing, or talent.

**Focus** applies either cost or differentiation to a narrow market segment. A focus strategy succeeds by serving a niche better than broad competitors can. Porter warned that firms failing to commit to one strategy get **stuck in the middle** — too expensive for cost-conscious buyers, too generic for quality-seeking ones.

steps: Firm analyses competitive environment
Chooses cost, differentiation, or focus
Aligns all operations to that choice
body.result: Clear competitive advantage — or 'stuck in the middle' if no choice is made

sections.title: Porter's Generic Strategies
sections.keyIdea: Porter argues every firm must choose: compete on cost, compete on uniqueness, or focus on a niche — trying to do everything leaves the firm 'stuck in the middle' with no clear advantage.
sections.examMatters: A common evaluative question is whether Porter's 'stuck in the middle' concept is still valid. Use IKEA or Zara as evidence that some firms blend strategies successfully. Argue that advances in technology and supply-chain management may have made hybrid strategies more achievable than Porter originally believed.

realExample.text: IKEA challenges Porter by combining cost leadership with differentiation. Its flat-pack model and massive purchasing power deliver low costs, while Scandinavian design and the in-store experience create genuine differentiation. Some analysts argue IKEA is a focused differentiator targeting young, urban, price-conscious consumers.

sections.misconception: Students assume cost leadership means cheapest price. Wrong — cost leadership means lowest costs of production, which may be used for low pricing or for higher margins at market prices. Instead write: cost leadership is about the cost base, not the price tag; the firm decides whether to pass savings to consumers or keep them as profit.

takeaway: Ansoff's matrix: penetration (safe) → product dev → market dev → diversification (risky).
Porter's three strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, or focus — choose one clearly.
'Stuck in the middle' is Porter's warning against half-measures, though modern firms sometimes blend strategies.
Always apply these frameworks to the specific firm in the case study — description alone scores poorly.

steps: Define mission and vision
Set SMART corporate objectives
Cascade to functional objectives
flow.result: All departments aligned toward the same strategic goals

section_notes.title: Corporate Objectives and Mission

items.text: Mission statement — a written declaration of a firm's core purpose and values; it answers 'why do we exist?' and guides strategic direction.
Corporate objectives — quantifiable targets set at the top level of the business (e.g. 'achieve 15% market share by 2027'); they translate the mission into action.
Functional objectives — targets set by individual departments (marketing, finance, HR, operations) that support the corporate objectives.
SMART objectives — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound; the framework for writing effective business targets.
Objectives form a hierarchy: mission → corporate aims → corporate objectives → functional objectives → individual targets.
Well-aligned objectives ensure all departments pull in the same direction; misalignment leads to conflicting priorities and wasted resources.
Examiners expect you to evaluate whether a firm's stated objectives match its actual behaviour — mission statements are often aspirational rather than operational.

section_notes.keyIdea: A business mission defines its purpose and values, while corporate objectives translate that mission into measurable targets — every strategic decision should flow from this hierarchy.
takeaway: Mission → corporate objectives → functional objectives → individual targets.
SMART framework ensures objectives are measurable and actionable.
Evaluate whether stated objectives match actual business behaviour.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners test whether you can link objectives to strategy. Always connect a firm's strategic decision to its stated objectives and evaluate whether the objective is actually being achieved.
section_notes.misconception: Students treat mission statements as operational tools. Wrong because many mission statements are vague PR exercises. Instead write: mission statements set direction and values, but it is the SMART corporate objectives beneath them that drive measurable action.

steps: Audit internal strengths and weaknesses
Scan external opportunities and threats
Match strengths to opportunities in strategy
flow.result: A clear strategic direction based on evidence, not guesswork

section_notes.title: Strategy and SWOT Analysis

items.text: Strategy — the medium-to-long-term plan that sets out how a business will achieve its corporate objectives; it involves choosing where to compete and how to win.
SWOT analysis — a framework assessing internal Strengths and Weaknesses and external Opportunities and Threats to inform strategic decision-making.
Tactics — short-term actions and decisions that implement the strategy; strategy is the 'what', tactics are the 'how'.
SWOT links internal capabilities (S/W) to the external environment (O/T), helping the firm identify where it has a competitive advantage.
The best strategies match strengths to opportunities (e.g. a strong brand entering a growing market) or use strengths to mitigate threats.
SWOT is a starting point, not a conclusion. Examiners reward you for using it to justify a recommendation, not just listing four quadrants.
SWOT connects to Porter's competitive strategies and Ansoff's matrix — all three frameworks inform which strategic direction to take.

section_notes.keyIdea: Strategy is the plan for achieving objectives — SWOT analysis provides a structured framework for evaluating where the business stands and which strategic direction makes sense.
takeaway: SWOT: internal strengths/weaknesses + external opportunities/threats.
Match strengths to opportunities to form strategy.
Always apply SWOT to the case study — listing alone earns low marks.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to apply SWOT to the case study, not recite the framework. Identify specific S/W/O/T from the scenario, then use them to justify your strategic recommendation. A SWOT table with no analysis scores poorly.
section_notes.misconception: Students list SWOT factors without analysing them. Listing is not analysis. Instead write: always link SWOT to a recommendation — 'The firm's strong brand (S) combined with the growing Asian market (O) suggests it should pursue market development using Ansoff's matrix.'

steps: Assess existing products and markets
Choose strategic direction using Ansoff's matrix
Risk increases from penetration → diversification
flow.result: Strategic direction aligned to the firm's capabilities and risk appetite

section_notes.title: Strategic Direction: Ansoff's Matrix

items.text: Market penetration — selling more of existing products in existing markets (lowest risk); focus on increasing market share through pricing, promotion, or loyalty.
Product development — launching new products into existing markets (medium risk); leverages existing customer relationships and distribution channels.
Market development — selling existing products in new markets (medium risk); involves geographical expansion or targeting new customer segments.
Diversification — new products in new markets (highest risk); spreads risk but the firm operates outside its area of expertise.
Risk increases as you move away from the firm's core business — diversification is riskiest because the firm lacks experience in both the product and the market.
Examiners expect you to justify which Ansoff strategy a firm should choose using evidence from the case study: financial position, market conditions, competitive environment, and risk appetite.
Ansoff's matrix links to SWOT: match the firm's strengths and the market opportunities to determine which quadrant is most appropriate.

section_notes.keyIdea: Ansoff's matrix maps out four strategic directions based on whether a firm is selling existing or new products in existing or new markets — each direction carries different levels of risk and reward.
takeaway: Ansoff's four strategies: penetration, product dev, market dev, diversification.
Risk increases moving away from existing products and markets.
Always justify your recommendation using case study evidence.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners ask you to recommend and justify an Ansoff strategy. Don't just name the quadrant — explain why it fits: 'Given the firm's strong cash position (SWOT) and the saturated UK market, market development into Southeast Asia would leverage its existing product range while accessing high-growth markets.'
section_notes.misconception: Students say diversification is always bad because it's risky. Wrong because diversification spreads risk across multiple revenue streams and can be highly profitable if managed well (e.g. Virgin Group). Instead write: diversification is the riskiest option but may be justified when existing markets are declining or the firm has excess resources to invest.

steps: Choose: compete on cost or differentiation
Choose scope: broad market or niche
Stuck in the middle = no competitive advantage
flow.result: Clear competitive advantage through cost, differentiation, or focus

section_notes.title: Competitive Strategy: Porter's Generic Strategies

items.text: Cost leadership — being the lowest-cost producer in the industry, enabling the firm to compete on price or earn higher margins at the market price.
Differentiation — creating a product that is perceived as unique (quality, design, brand, service), allowing the firm to charge a premium price.
Focus (niche) — targeting a narrow market segment with either a cost focus or differentiation focus strategy.
Being stuck in the middle means having neither the lowest costs nor a differentiated product — the firm has no clear competitive advantage and earns below-average returns.
In practice, some firms successfully combine cost and differentiation (e.g. IKEA: stylish furniture at low cost). Porter's model may be too rigid for dynamic markets.
Porter's strategies link to Ansoff's matrix: cost leadership often pairs with market penetration; differentiation pairs with product development.

section_notes.keyIdea: Porter argues that firms must choose between competing on cost or differentiation, across a broad or narrow market — trying to do everything leads to being 'stuck in the middle' with no competitive advantage.
takeaway: Cost leadership, differentiation, or focus — choose one for competitive advantage.
Stuck in the middle = no clear advantage = below-average returns.
Real-world firms sometimes combine strategies (IKEA model).
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to identify which Porter strategy a firm is using and evaluate whether it is sustainable. Use evidence: low prices suggest cost leadership; premium pricing and branding suggest differentiation.
section_notes.misconception: Students say a firm must choose one strategy and never change. Wrong because firms can shift strategy in response to market changes. Instead write: while Porter argues firms should commit to one strategy, in practice firms may evolve — the key is maintaining a clear competitive advantage at any given time.

section_quiz.question: Which level of business planning is the MOST specific and measurable?
section_quiz.explanation: Corporate objectives are SMART targets — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. Mission statements and aims are broader and more qualitative.

section_quiz.question: A business selling its existing product in a new country is pursuing which Ansoff strategy?
section_quiz.explanation: Market development involves taking an existing product into a new market — in this case, a new geographical market (country).

section_quiz.question: According to Porter, a firm that fails to adopt a clear generic strategy risks being:
section_quiz.explanation: Porter argued that firms without a clear strategy of cost leadership, differentiation, or focus end up 'stuck in the middle' with no competitive advantage.

section_quiz.question: In the BCG Matrix, which category describes a product with high market share in a low-growth market?
section_quiz.explanation: Cash cows have high market share in mature (low-growth) markets. They generate strong cash flows with minimal investment needed.

section_quiz.question: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL factor in a SWOT analysis?
section_quiz.explanation: A new competitor is an external threat. Skilled workforce, brand image, and efficient production are all internal strengths.

section_quiz.question: Which PESTLE factor would 'an increase in the national minimum wage' fall under?
section_quiz.explanation: The national minimum wage is set by legislation, making it a legal factor. It could also have economic implications, but the primary classification is legal.

section_quiz.question: According to Porter's Five Forces, which force is MOST affected by brand loyalty?
section_quiz.explanation: Strong brand loyalty acts as a barrier to entry — new entrants struggle to attract customers who are loyal to established brands.

section_quiz.question: A decision to acquire a rival business would be classified as:
section_quiz.explanation: Acquiring a rival is a major strategic decision — it is long-term, involves significant resources, is made by senior management, and is difficult to reverse.

options: They are too specific and restrictive
They are often vague and disconnected from actual behaviour
They are only useful for small businesses
section_quiz.question: Which criticism of mission statements is MOST valid?
section_quiz.explanation: The most common and valid criticism is that mission statements are often vague, generic, and may not reflect how the business actually operates.

section_quiz.question: Porter's Five Forces is best used to analyse:
section_quiz.explanation: Five Forces analyses the competitive intensity and attractiveness of an industry. Internal strengths are SWOT, product portfolio is BCG, and macro-environment is PESTLE.

section_practice.guidance: A mission statement is a broad qualitative statement of a business's overall purpose, values and reason for existing (1 mark). A corporate objective is a specific, measurable target derived from the mission that the business aims to achieve within a set timeframe (1 mark). For example, a mission might be 'to provide the best customer experience in retail', while a corporate objective might be 'to increase customer satisfaction scores by 10% within two years' (1 mark). The key difference is that missions are aspirational and general, while objectives are quantifiable and time-bound (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Define the term 'mission statement' and explain how it differs from a corporate objective. (4 marks)

section_practice.guidance: Strengths: skilled workforce and strong customer service reputation give NovaTech a basis for differentiation (1 mark). Weaknesses: higher costs than larger competitors and limited scale restrict price competitiveness (1 mark). Opportunities: growing demand for IT services and potential to specialise in high-value niches where expertise is rewarded (1 mark). Threats: continued price competition from larger firms and risk of losing key staff (1 mark). SWOT helps NovaTech identify that competing on price is unwise — instead, it should focus on differentiation through quality and specialist expertise (1 mark). Limitation: SWOT is subjective and does not prioritise factors or indicate the best course of action without further analysis (1 mark).
section_practice.question: NovaTech is a medium-sized IT services company facing increased price competition from larger firms, despite having a highly skilled workforce and strong reputation for customer service. Analyse how a SWOT analysis could help NovaTech develop its strategic direction. (6 marks)

section_practice.guidance: The conflict: shareholders want short-term returns through dividends and share price growth, which may require cost-cutting (2 marks). Long-term R&D investment reduces current profits but is essential for future revenue streams — pharmaceutical products take years to develop and bring to market (2 marks). Cutting R&D may boost short-term profits but weakens the product pipeline and threatens future competitiveness (2 marks). Possible solutions: clear communication of the long-term strategy to shareholders, balanced investment approaches, performance metrics that reward both short-term efficiency and long-term innovation (2 marks). Judgement: in pharmaceuticals, where product pipelines take 10-15 years to develop, the conflict is particularly acute — short-termism is especially damaging but shareholder pressure is difficult to resist (2 marks).
section_practice.question: A publicly listed pharmaceutical company is under pressure from shareholders to increase quarterly profits, while the R&D department is requesting a significant budget increase for a drug development programme that will not generate revenue for at least five years. Assess the potential conflict between short-term and long-term business objectives. (10 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Introduction: Define strategic direction and its components — mission, vision, objectives and strategy (2 marks).

For importance: provides focus and alignment across the organisation, ensuring resources are allocated effectively (3 marks); essential during leadership transitions when direction may become unclear without formal strategy — the family disagreement illustrates this risk (2 marks); investors, lenders and employees value strategic clarity (2 marks); helps the business respond proactively to market changes rather than drifting reactively (2 marks).

Against: some businesses succeed through flexibility and opportunism — the furniture firm has survived 30 years without formal strategy (2 marks); Mintzberg's emergent strategy suggests strategy evolves through experience rather than being rigidly planned in advance (2 marks); formal strategy development can be costly and time-consuming, and strategies can become outdated in dynamic markets (2 marks).

Evaluation: The transition point from founder to next generation specifically demands a formal strategy because the implicit direction provided by the founder is being lost. Each of the three proposed options (international expansion, online retailing, domestic focus) carries different risks using Ansoff's Matrix, and without strategic clarity the business risks pursuing all three ineffectively. However, the strategy should be flexible enough to adapt as circumstances change (3 marks).
section_practice.question: A family-owned furniture manufacturing business has grown organically over 30 years without a formal strategy. The founder is retiring and the next generation disagree about whether to expand internationally, move into online retailing, or maintain the current domestic focus. Evaluate the importance of having a clear strategic direction for the long-term success of a business. (20 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Reason 1: Changes in the external environment — such as new legislation, economic recession, or intensified competition — may make existing objectives unrealistic or irrelevant (1 mark), forcing the business to set new targets that reflect current conditions (1 mark).

Reason 2: A change in ownership or leadership — such as a takeover or new CEO — may bring different priorities and strategic vision (1 mark), leading to revised objectives that reflect the new direction (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Outline two reasons why a business might change its corporate objectives. (4 marks)

steps: A business sets SMART corporate objectives — specific, measurable targets such as increasing revenue by 15% within two years.
Clear objectives enable managers to allocate resources effectively and set aligned functional objectives for each department.
Employees understand what is expected, improving motivation, coordination and accountability across the organisation.
Progress can be monitored against benchmarks, enabling corrective action if targets are not being met.
chains.title: SMART objectives drive strategic direction
chains.result: SMART objectives provide the foundation for strategic planning — without clear goals, resource allocation becomes unfocused and performance cannot be measured.

steps: Market penetration (existing product, existing market) is lowest risk — increasing share through marketing or pricing.
Market development (existing product, new market) and product development (new product, existing market) carry moderate risk.
Diversification (new product, new market) is highest risk — the firm lacks experience in both the product and market.
The matrix helps managers choose a growth strategy that matches the firm's risk appetite and available resources.
chains.title: Ansoff's Matrix frames growth strategy risk
chains.result: Ansoff's Matrix provides a framework for evaluating growth options — the appropriate strategy depends on the firm's capabilities and willingness to accept risk.

steps: Cost leadership aims to be the lowest-cost producer through economies of scale, lean production and process efficiency.
Differentiation creates unique value through quality, branding, innovation or customer service — justifying premium prices.
Focus strategies target a narrow segment with either low cost or differentiation, avoiding direct competition with larger firms.
Porter argues firms must commit to one strategy — being 'stuck in the middle' leads to weak competitive positioning.
chains.title: Porter's generic strategies define competitive positioning
chains.result: Porter's model clarifies that competitive advantage comes from either cost or differentiation — firms must make a clear strategic choice.

steps: SWOT identifies internal strengths and weaknesses alongside external opportunities and threats.
Matching strengths to opportunities (e.g. strong brand + growing digital demand = launch e-commerce) creates focused strategy.
Addressing weaknesses that expose the firm to threats (e.g. weak cash flow + rising costs = restructure finance) prevents failure.
SWOT provides a simple framework for ensuring strategy is grounded in the firm's actual position, not wishful thinking.
chains.title: SWOT analysis links internal capability to external opportunity
chains.result: SWOT analysis ensures strategic decisions are evidence-based — it connects what the firm can do to what the market demands.

evaluation.title: Ansoff's Matrix oversimplifies strategic choice
evaluation.content: The matrix presents only four options and ignores resources, capabilities and competitive context. A 'high-risk' diversification may be low risk for a firm with strong finances and transferable skills. Many firms pursue hybrid strategies that blend categories.

evaluation.title: Porter's 'stuck in the middle' is debatable
evaluation.content: Many successful firms combine cost efficiency with differentiation — Zara offers fast-fashion differentiation at relatively low prices. The model provides a useful starting point but must be adapted to the specific competitive context.

evaluation.title: Stakeholder conflicts complicate objective-setting
evaluation.content: Shareholders want profit maximisation; employees want higher wages; customers want lower prices. Corporate objectives inevitably involve trade-offs depending on stakeholder power. The most sustainable strategies balance multiple interests rather than prioritising one group.

section_common_mistakes.title: Listing SWOT Factors Without Analysis
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Examiners award marks for application and analysis, not just identification. A SWOT list with no strategic discussion scores poorly.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Simply listing strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats without explaining their strategic implications.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Use SWOT as a tool for developing strategy — explain HOW the firm should exploit strengths and opportunities, and HOW it should address weaknesses and threats. Link SWOT to specific recommendations.

section_common_mistakes.title: Describing PESTLE Factors Generically
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Generic PESTLE descriptions earn minimal marks. Application to the specific business context is essential for higher marks.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Writing general statements like 'economic factors affect the business' without applying them to the specific case study.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always specify WHICH economic factor (e.g. rising interest rates), HOW it affects the business (e.g. increases borrowing costs for expansion), and WHAT the strategic implication is (e.g. may delay growth plans).

section_common_mistakes.title: Treating Ansoff Strategies as Equally Risky
section_common_mistakes.examTip: A strong answer will evaluate whether the risk of a chosen strategy is appropriate given the firm's resources, market position, and competitive environment.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Failing to distinguish between the risk levels of different Ansoff strategies.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always explain that risk increases from market penetration (lowest) through to diversification (highest). Justify your assessment by explaining WHY each strategy carries its level of risk.

section_common_mistakes.title: Confusing Porter's Five Forces with PESTLE
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Use PESTLE for macro-environment, Five Forces for industry competition, and SWOT to link external analysis to internal capabilities.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Mixing up industry-level competitive analysis (Five Forces) with macro-environmental analysis (PESTLE).
section_common_mistakes.correction: Five Forces analyses the competitive intensity WITHIN an industry (suppliers, buyers, rivals, entrants, substitutes). PESTLE analyses the WIDER external environment (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental).

section_common_mistakes.title: Ignoring Limitations of Strategic Models
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Evaluation marks require you to critique the models you use. Acknowledging limitations shows sophisticated understanding.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Presenting Ansoff, Porter, BCG, or SWOT as if they provide definitive answers to strategic questions.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always acknowledge limitations — these are simplifications of complex reality. They depend on accurate data, may be static snapshots, and do not account for all variables. Use them as starting points for analysis.

section_common_mistakes.title: Not Distinguishing Strategic from Tactical Decisions
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Case study questions often require you to identify whether a decision is strategic or tactical and evaluate its resource implications.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Treating all business decisions as equally important without classifying them as strategic or tactical.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Strategic decisions are long-term, resource-intensive, and set by senior management (e.g. entering a new market). Tactical decisions are short-term and operational (e.g. changing an advertising campaign). Always classify decisions in your analysis.
